# 2 Samuel Chapter 13 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 182r–183r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_013_page_001.jpg, 2SA_013_page_002.jpg, 2SA_013_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Now after this, Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister whose name was Tamar, and Amnon the son of David loved her.

**2** Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill on account of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.

**3** But Amnon had a friend whose name was Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, and Jonadab was a very shrewd man.

**4** He said to him, "Why are you so haggard, son of the king, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

**5** Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and prepare food for me. Let her make the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat from her hand.'"

**6** So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of heart-shaped cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."

**7** Then David sent word to Tamar at the palace, saying, "Go now to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare food for him."

**8** So Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, where he was lying down. She took dough and kneaded it and shaped the cakes in his sight and baked them.

**9** Then she took the pan and set them before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send everyone out from me." So everyone went out from him.

**10** Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the inner chamber, that I may eat from your hand." So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the inner chamber.

**11** When she brought them near to him to eat, he seized her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."

**12** She said to him, "No, my brother, do not force me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing.

**13** As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."

**14** But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she, and he forced her and lay with her.

**15** Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred, for the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!"

**16** She said to him, "No — for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.

**17** He called his servant who attended him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."

**18** Now she was wearing a robe of long sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king clothed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her.

**19** And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the robe of long sleeves that was on her. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.

**20** And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Be silent for now, my sister — he is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart." So Tamar remained, desolate, in the house of her brother Absalom.

**21** When King David heard all these things, he was very angry.

**22** But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon because he had forced his sister Tamar.

**23** After two full years, Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the sons of the king.

**24** Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."

**25** But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be a burden to you." He pressed him, but he would not go, yet he gave him his blessing.

**26** Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." The king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"

**27** But Absalom pressed him until he sent Amnon and all the sons of the king with him.

**28** And Absalom commanded his servants, saying, "Watch — when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and I say to you, 'Strike Amnon!' — then kill him. Do not fear. Have I not commanded you? Be strong and be men of valor."

**29** So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the sons of the king rose, and each mounted his mule and fled.

**30** While they were on the way, a report came to David: "Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king, and not one of them is left."

**31** Then the king rose and tore his garments and lay on the ground, and all his servants stood by with their garments torn.

**32** But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, answered and said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the sons of the king, for Amnon alone is dead. By the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he forced his sister Tamar.

**33** Now therefore, let not my lord the king take it to heart, thinking all the sons of the king are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."

**34** Meanwhile Absalom fled. The young man who kept watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming along the road behind him from the hillside.

**35** And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the sons of the king have come; as your servant said, so it has come to pass."

**36** As soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the sons of the king came and lifted up their voices and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.

**37** But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.

**38** So Absalom fled and went to Geshur and remained there three years.

**39** And the spirit of King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted concerning Amnon, since he was dead.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the narrative structure and the devastating emotional arc of this chapter: Amnon's obsession (vv.1-5), the trap and rape (vv.6-14), the reversal and expulsion (vv.15-19), the aftermath and silence (vv.20-22), and Absalom's calculated revenge (vv.23-39). The key literary devices — the *ketonet passim* echo, the love-hatred reversal, and Absalom's ominous silence — are recognized by all three. The Masoretic text is the primary base, though the LXX addition at v.21 is noted by all translators as likely preserving an original reading.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "Now after this" vs. "Some time later" vs. "And-it-was after thus"
- **EMET:** "And-it-was after thus"
- **LOGOS:** "Now after this"
- **PNEUMA:** "Some time later, trouble came from within David's own house"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Now after this." LOGOS captures the Hebrew *vayehi acharey-khen* formally while remaining readable. PNEUMA's addition of "trouble came from within David's own house" is interpretive — accurate, but not in the text.

### V.2 — "tormented" vs. "distressing" vs. "obsessed"
- **EMET:** "And-it-was-distressing [vayetser] to-Amnon"
- **LOGOS:** "Amnon was so tormented"
- **PNEUMA:** "Amnon was so obsessed"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Amnon was so tormented." LOGOS best captures *vayetser* (the pressing, constricting nature of the anguish) without the modern clinical connotation of PNEUMA's "obsessed."

### V.3 — "wise" vs. "shrewd" vs. "clever"
- **EMET:** "a-man very wise [chakham]"
- **LOGOS:** "a very shrewd man"
- **PNEUMA:** "a very clever man"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "a very shrewd man." The Hebrew *chakham* means "wise," but context demands a term that captures the morally ambiguous application of wisdom. LOGOS's "shrewd" balances accuracy with narrative irony. EMET's literal "wise" is misleading in English.

### V.4 — "thin" vs. "haggard" vs. "worse"
- **EMET:** "Why [are]-you thus thin [dal]"
- **LOGOS:** "Why are you so haggard"
- **PNEUMA:** "Day after day you look worse"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Why are you so haggard." The Hebrew *dal* means thin/low/poor. LOGOS's "haggard" captures the visible physical deterioration implied by the word.

### V.14 — "forced her" vs. "overpowered her and raped her"
- **EMET:** "and-he-forced-her [vay'anneha] and-lay with-her"
- **LOGOS:** "he forced her and lay with her"
- **PNEUMA:** "he overpowered her and raped her"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "he forced her and lay with her." The Hebrew uses two verbs: *vay'anneha* (he forced/afflicted her) and *vayishkav otah* (he lay with her). LOGOS preserves the dual-verb structure. PNEUMA's "raped" is accurate but the Hebrew deliberately uses the verb *'anah* (to afflict/force) which carries broader covenantal overtones.

### V.15 — "Get up! Go!" vs. "Arise, go!" vs. "Get up! Get out!"
- **EMET:** "Arise, go!"
- **LOGOS:** "Get up! Go!"
- **PNEUMA:** "Get up! Get out!"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Get up! Go!" — LOGOS's rendering captures the brutal brevity of *qumiy lekhi* with appropriate force.

### V.16 — Tamar's protest: greater/lesser evil
- **EMET:** "this evil, the great, [is]-greater-than the other"
- **LOGOS:** "this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other"
- **PNEUMA:** "Throwing me out like this is an even greater wrong"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." LOGOS clarifies the Hebrew construction while staying close to the text. Tamar argues that the public dismissal compounds the private violation.

### V.17 — "this one" vs. "this woman"
- **EMET:** "Send-out, please, this-one from-upon-me"
- **LOGOS:** "Put this woman out of my presence"
- **PNEUMA:** "Get this woman out of here"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Put this woman out of my presence." The Hebrew *et-zot* means "this one" (feminine). LOGOS correctly identifies the dehumanizing force of the pronoun — Amnon refers to Tamar as "this one/this woman" rather than by name.

### V.19 — "crying aloud" vs. "crying out" vs. "wailing"
- **EMET:** "walking and-crying-out [za'aqah]"
- **LOGOS:** "crying aloud as she went"
- **PNEUMA:** "wailing as she went"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "crying aloud as she went." The Hebrew *za'aqah* is a loud public cry — stronger than weeping, associated with appeals for justice. LOGOS's "crying aloud" preserves the public nature of the outcry. PNEUMA's "wailing" is close but carries more connotation of grief than protest.

### V.20 — "Be silent" vs. "Be quiet for now"
- **EMET:** "be-silent [hacharishiy]"
- **LOGOS:** "Now be silent, my sister"
- **PNEUMA:** "Be quiet for now, sister"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Be silent for now, my sister." Combining LOGOS's formal "be silent" with PNEUMA's temporal "for now." The Hebrew *hacharishiy* means "be silent/hold your peace" — Absalom's instruction may be protective (don't expose yourself to more shame) or tactical (wait for my plan).

### V.21 — LXX addition
- **EMET:** Notes the LXX addition in textual notes
- **LOGOS:** Notes the LXX addition in translation notes
- **PNEUMA:** "But he did nothing" (incorporates the LXX sense into the translation text)
- **SOPHIA ruling:** The consensus translation follows the MT ("he was very angry") without the LXX addition in the verse itself. PNEUMA's interpolation "But he did nothing," while historically defensible, goes beyond the Masoretic base text. The LXX reading is discussed in the Council Notes.

### V.37 — "mourned for his son" — which son?
- **EMET:** "And-he-mourned over his-son all the-days"
- **LOGOS:** "And David mourned for his son day after day"
- **PNEUMA:** "And David grieved for his son every day"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "And David mourned for his son day after day." The ambiguity of "his son" (Amnon? Absalom? both?) is deliberate in the Hebrew and should not be resolved by the translator. LOGOS's phrasing preserves this ambiguity while maintaining dignity.

### V.39 — "longed" and subject of the verb
- **EMET:** "And-longed [vatekhal] the-spirit [ruach] of-the-king David to-go-out to Avshalom"
- **LOGOS:** "the spirit of King David longed to go out to Absalom"
- **PNEUMA:** "the heart of King David ached to go to Absalom"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the spirit of King David longed to go out to Absalom." LOGOS/EMET correctly identify the verb *vatekhal* (to be consumed/long) and supply *ruach* as the implicit feminine subject. PNEUMA's "heart... ached" is evocative but substitutes a different organ and verb.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
